title: The Chesterfield aftermath and Redd Foxx's thanks at the Apollo
summary: Union arguments that Black players cannot read are answered; twenty years later Redd Foxx thanks Maxwell for the Chesterfield stand.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: that. What was that you were telling me about, an opposite story about what had happened to you before and what happened to you when you were with Redd Foxx?

Oh, yeah, going back to that story with the Chesterfield story and, you know, taking that case up to the union. While -- it reminds me of other stuff, too. First, while we were at the union these guys were saying, well, it's not that we're prejudiced against the black guys. But you know how it is, the black guy's a jazz musician, he can't read. And, you know, they're troublemakers. And Feinberg said, "Well, I've got a white, Anglo-Saxon man sitting here, Protestant -- he didn't know I'm not a protestant, who brought the charges up. The black guys did not bring the charges up, this white man did. So why don't you ask him about whether they can read." I said, "Well, Teddy Wilson is going to give a concert in Town Hall with Vera Landaska this week. Now, she's going to be very surprised to find out he can't read. And Charlie Shavers has played with this band and that band, first trumpet player." I said it was one of the most ridiculous accusations I had ever heard.

So repercussions went on through the years but the nicest one was 20 years later, I was playing at the Apollo Theater with Quincy Jones and Redd Foxx was the star, Billy Eckstine and Redd Foxx. And the last night -- well, Redd Foxx always kidded me, looked back and called me "The Lord," because
I had long hair. He said, "I knew everything was all right when I saw the Lord back there in the trumpet section."
And one morning Gertrude came in with me and he's sitting in the stage door and he says, "Morning, Jesus, Morning, Mary."

But it was that kind of thing. You know, just a joke back and forth. And the last night Jerome came down, Richardson, he was the contractor. He said, "Redd wants to see you up in his dressing room." I said, "Why?" And he said, "I don't know, I didn't ask him." So I went up. Redd said, sit down, have a drink, he gave me a drink. He said, "You know, I've been hearing about you from black musicians for years." And I said, "What do you mean?" He said, "That thing you did 20 years ago with the Chesterfield thing, with the radio program." And he said, "I always wanted to shake hands and say thank you. I read about it at the time." It was in the Amsterdam News. What was the name of that guy, he was a piano player, wrote a column for the Amsterdam News ?

Dan Burley, yeah. He wrote a nice column about me. And he said he'd read it and he'd always heard about me and he wanted to meet me and shake my hand and thank me. And, you know, I'm very emotional. I started to cry. But
it was like it almost made it worthwhile, somebody thought I did -- I thought, Well, Jesus, once in a while I do something right in my life.
